title: AVD Networking: VNets, Required Endpoints, RDP Shortpath, and Private Link
monthTitle: Azure Virtual Desktop Infrastructure: Plan, Deploy & Scale
summary: Session hosts live in your virtual network, so networking design decisions directly shape user experience and security posture. This lesson covers how to design a VNet and subnet for AVD, the exact outbound connectivity a session host needs (service tags and required FQDNs), how RDP Shortpath establishes a direct UDP path for managed and public networks, when to use Private Link instead of public endpoints, and how to plan bandwidth and hybrid connectivity for real workloads.
objectives: Design a VNet and subnet layout for AVD session hosts that supports growth and hybrid connectivity
List the outbound connectivity AVD session hosts require, using the WindowsVirtualDesktop service tag and required FQDNs
Explain how RDP Shortpath for managed networks differs from RDP Shortpath for public networks
Explain when and why to deploy Azure Private Link for AVD instead of relying on public service endpoints
Estimate per-user bandwidth needs for different workload types and plan hybrid connectivity accordingly

quiz.q: Which Azure networking construct lets you allow AVD traffic through an NSG or Azure Firewall without maintaining a list of Microsoft's changing IP ranges yourself?
options: A user-defined route pointing to 0.0.0.0/0
A private endpoint on the session host's NIC
An application security group scoped to the session host subnet
The WindowsVirtualDesktop service tag (and matching FQDN tag on Azure Firewall)
quiz.why: Azure publishes AVD's required endpoints as the WindowsVirtualDesktop service tag for NSGs/UDRs and the matching FQDN tag for Azure Firewall, so you reference the tag in your rule instead of hardcoding IP ranges that Microsoft manages and changes over time.

quiz.q: A session host's NSG blocks outbound access to *.blob.core.windows.net and *.servicebus.windows.net, but allows the WindowsVirtualDesktop service tag. What is the likely result?
options: Users will experience broken agent registration or session functionality, because those storage/service-bus endpoints carry diagnostics, agent updates, and other required traffic not covered by the service tag alone
No impact — the service tag alone covers all AVD requirements
The host will fail to boot
RDP Shortpath will silently fall back to TCP with no other effect
quiz.why: The WindowsVirtualDesktop service tag covers the core static AVD endpoints, but Microsoft's required-FQDN guidance calls out that you must still separately allow specific storage and Service Bus endpoints used for agent communication and diagnostics. Blocking them breaks functionality even with the service tag allowed.

quiz.q: What is the key architectural difference between RDP Shortpath for managed networks and RDP Shortpath for public networks?
options: Managed networks always use TCP; public networks always use UDP

Managed networks establish a direct UDP connection over a private network path (like VPN or ExpressRoute) and can use a listener on the host; public networks establish a direct UDP connection over the public internet using ICE/STUN, with TURN as a relay fallback when a direct path can't be negotiated
Public networks require Azure Front Door; managed networks do not
There is no difference — 'managed' and 'public' are marketing terms for the same underlying protocol
quiz.why: RDP Shortpath for managed networks uses a private connection (ExpressRoute private peering or VPN) and can use a direct UDP listener on the session host. RDP Shortpath for public networks negotiates a direct UDP path across the internet using ICE/STUN; when a direct path is blocked by NAT or firewalls, it can fall back to a relayed connection via TURN so the session still gets a UDP transport instead of dropping to TCP.

quiz.q: Why would an organization deploy Azure Private Link for Azure Virtual Desktop rather than relying on the default public endpoints?
options: Private Link is required before you can create any host pool
Private Link replaces the need for RDP Shortpath entirely

It routes the AVD control-plane traffic (feed discovery, feed download, and/or session connections, depending on configuration) over private endpoints in the customer's VNet instead of the public internet, supporting stricter network isolation requirements
Private Link is only relevant for personal host pools
quiz.why: Private Link for AVD lets you route parts of the AVD connection sequence over a private endpoint inside your VNet, which matters for organizations with strict network isolation or compliance requirements that prohibit public internet exposure. Note that public-network RDP Shortpath (STUN/TURN) is not supported when Private Link is in use for the session connection — you use RDP Shortpath for managed networks instead.

quiz.q: You need to size a VPN or ExpressRoute circuit for a group of 200 concurrent AVD users doing general knowledge-work (office apps, web, light video). What is the correct planning approach?
options: Assume zero bandwidth, since AVD traffic never leaves the session host's VNet
Always provision for the maximum theoretical bandwidth of the display protocol regardless of workload
Bandwidth planning is unnecessary because RDP Shortpath removes all bandwidth constraints

Use Microsoft's published RDP bandwidth requirement guidance per workload type as a starting per-user estimate, multiply by expected concurrent users, and validate with a pilot before finalizing circuit sizing
quiz.why: Microsoft publishes RDP bandwidth requirement guidance broken out by usage pattern (light office work vs. video-heavy workloads). The practical approach is to use that guidance as a per-user baseline, scale it to your expected concurrency, and then validate against a pilot group before committing to a circuit size — bandwidth needs vary significantly by real usage.

quiz.q: In two to four sentences, describe the outbound-only connectivity model a session host subnet needs for AVD to function, and name one specific type of endpoint beyond the WindowsVirtualDesktop service tag that must also be explicitly allowed.
quiz.answer: A session host subnet only needs outbound connectivity — no inbound rule is required for AVD connectivity itself because the AVD agent initiates an outbound connection to the service (reverse connect). The NSG or firewall should allow outbound access to the WindowsVirtualDesktop service tag (or FQDN tag on Azure Firewall) for the core control-plane endpoints. Beyond that, Microsoft's required-FQDN list calls out specific storage and messaging endpoints — for example *.blob.core.windows.net and *.servicebus.windows.net — that carry agent communication, diagnostics, and other required traffic and must be allowed separately, in addition to whatever endpoints the session host's applications and OS patching need.
quiz.why: AVD's networking model is outbound-only by design (reverse connect), but the required connectivity is broader than the service tag alone — the storage and Service Bus endpoints used for agent telemetry and communication are a commonly missed piece that causes registration or session failures when locked down too aggressively.

body_markdown:
## Why Networking Is Not an Afterthought

Because session hosts are customer-managed VMs sitting in your own virtual network, every networking decision you make — subnet sizing, firewall rules, transport protocol, hybrid connectivity — directly shows up as either a smooth remote desktop experience or a stream of "my session feels laggy" tickets. This lesson gives you the four pieces you need: how to lay out the VNet, what outbound connectivity is actually required, how RDP Shortpath gets you a fast UDP path instead of plain TCP, and when Private Link changes the picture.

## Designing the VNet and Subnet

Start with the basics that apply to any VM fleet, then layer AVD-specific concerns on top:

- **Dedicate a subnet (or subnets) to session hosts** rather than mixing them with other workloads, so NSG rules, route tables, and monitoring stay scoped and readable. Segregating personal-pool hosts from pooled-pool hosts in separate subnets is a common pattern when their security posture or DR treatment differs.
- **Size for growth, not just day one.** Host pools scale by adding more session hosts, and a subnet that's too small forces a re-IP exercise later. Plan address space for at least your two-year headcount projection plus autoscale burst capacity.
- **Region alignment matters for latency.** Deploy session hosts in the Azure region closest to the majority of your users, not necessarily the region where the rest of your estate happens to live — user experience is dominated by round-trip time between client and host.

Your session host subnet is **outbound-only** by design, thanks to reverse connect (Lesson 1). That simplifies the inbound story to almost nothing, but it raises the bar on getting outbound rules exactly right.

## Required Outbound Connectivity

Microsoft publishes a required-FQDN list for AVD, and the practical way to consume it is:

- Use the **WindowsVirtualDesktop service tag** in your NSG or route table rules (or the matching **FQDN tag** if you're using Azure Firewall) to cover the core static AVD service endpoints — the broker, diagnostics, and related control-plane traffic — without hand-maintaining IP ranges Microsoft controls and changes.
- **Separately allow specific storage and messaging endpoints** that the service tag does not fully cover — Microsoft calls out endpoints such as `*.blob.core.windows.net`, `*.servicebus.windows.net`, and `*.table.core.windows.net` scoped to the specific deployment URLs used for agent communication, diagnostics, and telemetry. Skipping these is one of the most common causes of "the host registers but sessions behave oddly" tickets.
- Allow whatever your **image and applications** independently need: Windows Update or WSUS/Configuration Manager endpoints, your package management service, line-of-business API endpoints, and identity endpoints for Microsoft Entra ID authentication.
- Microsoft explicitly does **not support** AVD deployments where required FQDNs are blocked — treat the required list as non-negotiable, not a starting point for further lockdown.

## RDP Shortpath: Two Different Mechanisms

RDP Shortpath establishes a **direct UDP-based transport** between the client and the session host instead of relaying everything through the TCP-based reverse connect path — UDP tolerates packet loss and jitter far better than TCP for real-time audio/video and input, which is exactly what a remote desktop session needs. There are two distinct variants, and mixing them up is a common exam trap:

- **RDP Shortpath for managed networks**: used when the client reaches the session host over a network you control end-to-end — a site-to-site VPN or ExpressRoute private peering. It can use a listener configured directly on the session host, or fall back to ICE/STUN-based discovery when the listener isn't enabled and inbound ports aren't opened, to find a usable direct UDP path across that private network.
- **RDP Shortpath for public networks**: used when the client connects over the general internet, with no private network in common. It uses **ICE/STUN** to attempt a direct UDP connection first. When NAT or firewall behavior prevents a direct path, it can fall back to a **relayed connection via TURN**, which still gets the session a UDP transport instead of dropping all the way back to plain TCP. This works automatically, with no extra configuration, as long as your session hosts, clients, and any firewalls in between allow the traffic and RDP transport settings remain at their defaults.

The practical takeaway: managed-network Shortpath is for organizations with private connectivity already in place (VPN/ExpressRoute); public-network Shortpath with its ICE/STUN/TURN fallback chain is what makes remote, unmanaged, internet-connected users get a good UDP-based experience without you having to build private connectivity to every home office.

## Private Link: Keeping Traffic Off the Public Internet

**Azure Private Link for Azure Virtual Desktop** lets you expose the AVD service's connection endpoints — feed discovery, feed download, and/or the session connection itself, depending on which Private Link scenario you enable — through a **private endpoint** inside your own VNet, instead of the public AVD service endpoints. This matters for organizations with strict network isolation requirements (regulated industries, government, or any environment where "no path to the internet" is a hard requirement) who still want to use the managed AVD service.

Two things to remember when you combine Private Link with the rest of this lesson: first, Private Link for session connections requires the **entire TCP dynamic port range (1–65535)** open to the private endpoint, because port mapping happens through a single private IP for all the global gateway instances behind it. Second, **RDP Shortpath for public networks (STUN/TURN) is not supported** alongside Private Link for the session connection — if you need a direct UDP path in a Private Link deployment, you use **RDP Shortpath for managed networks** instead, over your private connectivity.

## Bandwidth Planning and Hybrid Connectivity

Bandwidth needs vary enormously by workload type — a data-entry task worker on a single monitor uses a small fraction of the bandwidth of a user running multiple 4K monitors with heavy video conferencing through the session. Rather than guessing, use Microsoft's published **RDP bandwidth requirements** guidance as a per-user starting point, broken out by usage pattern, and then:

1. Multiply the relevant per-user figure by your expected **concurrent** (not total) user count for the workload type you're sizing.
2. Add headroom for Teams media traffic if you're not offloading it (Teams optimization is covered in Module 5).
3. Validate against a real **pilot group** before finalizing a VPN or ExpressRoute circuit size — published guidance is a baseline, not a guarantee for your specific application mix.
4. For **hybrid connectivity** (on-prem file shares, line-of-business systems, domain controllers for hybrid-joined hosts), size the VPN gateway SKU or ExpressRoute circuit for the combined AVD session traffic and the backend traffic those sessions will generate, not just one or the other.

Getting the VNet layout, required connectivity, Shortpath configuration, and bandwidth sizing right up front is what turns AVD from "technically working" into an experience users don't think about — which is the actual bar for a production EUC platform.

slides.narration: Session hosts live in your own virtual network, which means every networking decision you make shows up directly in the user's experience. In this lesson we cover how to lay out the VNet, exactly what outbound connectivity AVD requires, how RDP Shortpath gets sessions onto a fast UDP path, when Private Link changes the picture, and how to plan bandwidth for real workloads.

slides.title: Designing the VNet and Subnet
bullets: Dedicate subnets to session hosts, separate personal from pooled
Size address space for two years of growth plus autoscale burst
Deploy in the region closest to your users, not your other workloads
The subnet is outbound-only thanks to reverse connect
slides.narration: Start with the fundamentals. Dedicate subnets to session hosts rather than mixing them with other workloads, and consider separating personal pool hosts from pooled hosts if their security posture differs. Size your address space for real growth, not just day one, because host pools scale by adding hosts and a too-small subnet forces a painful re-IP later. And deploy in the region closest to your actual users — round-trip latency dominates the user experience far more than proximity to the rest of your estate.

slides.title: Required Outbound Connectivity
bullets: Use the WindowsVirtualDesktop service tag for core endpoints
Separately allow storage and Service Bus endpoints for the agent
Also allow Windows Update, identity, and app endpoints
Microsoft does not support blocking required FQDNs
slides.narration: The WindowsVirtualDesktop service tag covers the core AVD control-plane endpoints in your NSG or firewall rules, without you having to track Microsoft's IP ranges yourself. But that tag alone isn't the whole story — you also need to separately allow specific storage and Service Bus endpoints that carry agent communication and diagnostics. Layer on whatever your image and applications independently need, like Windows Update and identity endpoints. Microsoft is explicit that blocking any required FQDN is not a supported configuration.

slides.title: RDP Shortpath: Direct UDP Transport
bullets: Establishes direct UDP instead of relaying over TCP
UDP tolerates packet loss and jitter far better for real-time input
Two distinct variants: managed networks and public networks
Getting the variant right is a common exam trap
slides.narration: RDP Shortpath's whole purpose is to get the session off the default TCP-based reverse connect path and onto a direct UDP transport, because UDP handles the packet loss and jitter of a real-time interactive session far better. There are two genuinely different variants depending on how the client reaches the host, and mixing them up is one of the most common mistakes candidates make on this topic.

slides.title: Shortpath for Managed Networks
bullets: Used over a private connection you control end to end
VPN site-to-site or ExpressRoute private peering
Can use a listener configured on the session host
Falls back to ICE/STUN discovery if the listener isn't enabled
slides.narration: RDP Shortpath for managed networks applies when the client reaches the session host over a network you control completely, like a site-to-site VPN or ExpressRoute private peering. It can use a direct listener configured on the session host itself, or fall back to ICE and STUN based discovery to find a usable direct UDP path across that private network if the listener isn't enabled and inbound ports aren't opened.

slides.title: Shortpath for Public Networks
bullets: Used when the client connects over the general internet
ICE/STUN attempts a direct UDP path first
TURN relay fallback when direct connection is blocked
Works automatically with default settings, no extra config
slides.narration: RDP Shortpath for public networks applies when there's no private network in common between client and host — just the general internet. It uses ICE and STUN to try to negotiate a direct UDP connection first. When NAT or firewall behavior blocks that direct path, it can fall back to a relayed connection through TURN, which still keeps the session on UDP instead of dropping all the way back to plain TCP. This works automatically as long as the defaults are in place and nothing in the path is blocking the traffic.

slides.title: Private Link: Off the Public Internet
bullets: Routes AVD connection stages through a private endpoint in your VNet
Fits strict network isolation or compliance requirements
Needs the full TCP dynamic port range open to the endpoint
Public-network Shortpath (STUN/TURN) is not supported with it
slides.narration: Private Link for Azure Virtual Desktop lets you route feed discovery, feed download, and the session connection itself through a private endpoint inside your own VNet instead of the public AVD service endpoints, which matters for organizations with strict isolation requirements. Two things to remember: it needs the entire TCP dynamic port range open to that private endpoint, and public-network RDP Shortpath with STUN and TURN is not supported alongside it — if you need direct UDP in a Private Link deployment, you use Shortpath for managed networks instead.

slides.title: Bandwidth Planning by Workload
bullets: Bandwidth need varies hugely by workload type
Use Microsoft's published per-user guidance as a baseline
Multiply by expected concurrent users, not total headcount
Validate against a real pilot before sizing the circuit
slides.narration: A task worker on one monitor uses a fraction of the bandwidth of someone running multiple high-resolution monitors with heavy video conferencing through their session. Use Microsoft's published RDP bandwidth guidance, broken out by usage pattern, as your starting per-user estimate. Multiply by expected concurrent users, not your total headcount, and always validate against a real pilot group before you commit to a VPN or ExpressRoute circuit size.

slides.title: Sizing Hybrid Connectivity
bullets: Size for AVD session traffic plus backend traffic together
Domain controllers, file shares, and LOB systems add load
Don't size the circuit for AVD alone if hosts are hybrid-joined
Revisit sizing as the pilot group grows toward production
slides.narration: If your session hosts are hybrid-joined or need to reach on-premises file shares, domain controllers, or line-of-business systems, size your VPN gateway or ExpressRoute circuit for the combined AVD session traffic and that backend traffic together, not one in isolation. And treat your initial sizing as a starting point — revisit it as the pilot group scales toward full production.

slides.title: Bringing It Together
bullets: VNet layout shapes growth and manageability
Required connectivity is non-negotiable, not a lockdown target
Shortpath variant depends on how the client reaches the host
Private Link and bandwidth planning are compliance and UX levers
slides.narration: Networking for AVD comes down to four things working together: a VNet layout that supports growth, outbound connectivity that matches Microsoft's required list exactly, the right RDP Shortpath variant for how your users actually connect, and bandwidth and hybrid connectivity sized from real data rather than guesswork. Get these right and the display protocol lesson from Module 1 stops being theory and starts being the experience your users actually get.
